title: 27 — System Design Case Studies: How Real Products Work
html:
27 — System Design Case Studies: How Real Products Work

Six products people actually ask you to design, each taken to the level where the interesting decision lives.

08 §8 covers the generic warm-ups — URL shortener, rate limiter, news feed fan-out. This file assumes those and does not repeat them. Where a product depends on one (Instagram on fan-out), it says so and moves on to what is specific to that product.

Sources are listed at the end. Where a number comes from a published engineering account it is marked [n]; where it is an order-of-magnitude estimate for interview arithmetic, it says so.

How to use these

An interviewer does not want a recital. They want to see you find the one hard problem and reason about it. Every study below is organised around that:

  1. Requirements — functional, then the non-functional one that actually shapes the design
  2. The hard problem — the single constraint everything else follows from
  3. Architecture — a diagram you could redraw on a whiteboard in ninety seconds
  4. Decisions — with the alternative and why it loses
  5. Failure modes — say these unprompted
  6. What to say — the two sentences that land

1. WhatsApp — messaging at planetary scale

Requirements

Functional Non-functional
1:1 and group messaging Hundreds of millions of simultaneously connected devices
Delivery receipts (sent / delivered / read) End-to-end encrypted — the server cannot read content
Media attachments Ordered delivery per conversation
Offline delivery when the device returns Tiny operational team

The hard problem

Not throughput — concurrency. Every online phone holds an open connection permanently, because a push must arrive in milliseconds without polling. So the question is: what does one idle connection cost you?

A thread-per-connection model costs ~1 MB of stack each; a million connections is a terabyte of RAM before a single message moves. This is why the answer is an event loop or a lightweight-process runtime, and why WhatsApp chose Erlang: a BEAM process costs roughly 300 bytes, and they reported around 2 million connections per server [1][2].

⚠️ This is the whole insight. "Use Erlang" is not the answer — "idle connections must cost hundreds of bytes, not megabytes, so I need lightweight processes or an event loop, not OS threads" is. C# gets there with async sockets over the thread pool; Go with goroutines; Node with libuv.

Architecture

flowchart LR
    P1[Phone A] -- persistent TLS --> GW[Connection gateway<br/>one lightweight process per device]
    P2[Phone B] -- persistent TLS --> GW
    GW --> SESS[(Session registry<br/>device to gateway node)]
    GW --> ROUTE[Message router]
    ROUTE --> QUEUE[(Offline queue<br/>per recipient)]
    ROUTE --> GW
    GW --> MEDIA[Media service]
    MEDIA --> BLOB[(Encrypted blob store + CDN)]

What happens when A messages B

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Phone A
    participant G as Gateway
    participant R as Router
    participant B as Phone B
    A->>G: encrypted payload plus client message id
    G->>R: route to recipient
    R->>R: "look up B in the session registry"
    alt B is online
        R->>B: deliver
        B-->>R: delivered receipt
    else B is offline
        R->>R: "persist to B's offline queue"
    end
    R-->>A: sent receipt
    Note over B: on reconnect B drains its queue

Decisions

Decision Choice Why not the alternative
Transport Persistent TCP/TLS, custom binary framing HTTP polling adds latency and battery cost; long-polling holds a connection anyway with more overhead
Concurrency Process/coroutine per connection Thread per connection dies at ~10k connections
Message storage Queue until delivered, then drop Storing all history server-side multiplies storage and creates a liability under E2E encryption
Ordering Per-conversation sequence number from the sender A global order is impossible and unnecessary
Group fan-out Server-side fan-out to N recipient queues Client-side fan-out costs the sender N uploads on a mobile link
Encryption E2E, keys never leave devices Server-side encryption lets the operator read messages

Failure modes

  • Gateway node dies — every device on it reconnects at once. Needs jittered client backoff, or you get a thundering herd that takes down the replacement.
  • Session registry is stale — a message routes to a gateway the device has left. Requires a fallback to the offline queue rather than a dropped message.
  • Duplicate delivery — retries after a lost ack mean the client must de-duplicate on the sender's message id. At-least-once plus idempotent clients, exactly as in 14 §3.

What to say

"The dominant cost is idle connections, not messages. I'd hold one lightweight process or async socket per device so an idle connection costs hundreds of bytes, keep a session registry mapping device to gateway node, and store messages only until delivery. Everything else — receipts, groups, media — hangs off that."

2. Instagram — media, feed and stories

Requirements

Functional Non-functional
Post a photo or video Feed p99 under ~200 ms
Home feed of followed accounts Read-dominated, roughly 100:1
Stories with 24-hour expiry Celebrity accounts with 100M+ followers
Explore / recommendations Global users, US-primary write region

The hard problem

The celebrity fan-out. Fan-out on write is right for the 99% — precompute each user's feed so a read is one lookup. But a post from an account with 100 million followers means 100 million queue writes for one action.

The answer is hybrid: fan-out on write for ordinary accounts, and for a small set of very-high-follower accounts, do not fan out at all — merge their recent posts in at read time. Every large social product converges on this. (The generic mechanics are in 08 §8.3; the celebrity split is the Instagram-specific part.)

Architecture

flowchart TB
    APP[Mobile app] --> LB[Edge and load balancer]
    LB --> API[API tier<br/>stateless]
    API --> GRAPH[(Social graph store<br/>follower edges)]
    API --> POSTS[(Post metadata<br/>wide-column)]
    API --> FEED[(Precomputed feed<br/>per user, capped)]
    API --> CACHE[(Memcache / Redis<br/>hot objects)]
    UP[Upload service] --> BLOB[(Blob store)]
    UP --> Q[[Transcode queue]]
    Q --> TRANS[Transcoder<br/>multiple sizes and formats]
    TRANS --> CDN[(CDN)]
    API -.celebrity posts merged at read.-> POSTS

Meta's published stack behind this: TAO for the social graph, Cassandra for key-value workloads including the photo feed, and Haystack for photo blobs [5][6]. Instagram later replaced Cassandra's storage engine with RocksDB — "Rocksandra" — to cut tail latency from JVM garbage collection [5].

Decisions

Decision Choice Why not the alternative
Feed generation Hybrid push/pull Pure push dies on celebrities; pure pull makes every read a scatter-gather over hundreds of accounts
Media storage Blob store + CDN, never the database Blobs in a relational database destroy the buffer pool and backup windows
Transcoding Async on upload, multiple renditions Transcoding inline makes the user wait seconds
Feed store Capped list per user (a few hundred entries) Unbounded feeds grow without limit and nobody scrolls that far
Stories Same pipeline, TTL on the row A separate subsystem duplicates the media path for no benefit
Write region Single master region, local queueing elsewhere Synchronous cross-ocean writes make European posts unusable [6]

⚠️ The upload path is the one people get wrong. The correct answer is: client uploads to blob storage (pre-signed URL, straight past your API tier), you write metadata, you enqueue transcoding, and the post becomes visible when the first rendition is ready. Streaming a 40 MB video through your API servers is the anti-pattern.

Failure modes

  • Transcode backlog — posts appear without playable media. Needs a visible "processing" state, not a broken tile.
  • Feed store and post store disagree — a deleted post still in feeds. Filter at read time; do not rely on fan-out deletion.
  • Cache stampede on a viral post — one recompute lock plus jittered TTL, as in 11 §5.

3. Netflix — video streaming

Requirements

Functional Non-functional
Browse catalogue, play any title Multi-terabit aggregate throughput
Adaptive quality on changing networks Start playback in ~1 second
Resume across devices Content is huge and mostly cold — a long tail nobody watches

The hard problem

Bytes, not requests. A social network's problem is many small requests; a streaming service's problem is sustained multi-gigabit delivery of the same large files. Serving that from central data centres would cost more in transit than the content itself.

So the design is inverted: push the content to the edge before anyone asks for it. Netflix built its own CDN, Open Connect, and places appliances inside ISP networks, provided free to qualifying ISPs — Netflix supplies the hardware, the ISP supplies power, space and connectivity [3][4]. Close to 95% of traffic is delivered over direct connections between Open Connect and the member's ISP [3].

Critically, the content is pre-positioned during off-peak "fill windows", not pulled on first miss [4]. A conventional CDN is demand-filled and reactive; this is predictive, because Netflix knows tomorrow's popularity better than a cache eviction policy does.

Architecture

flowchart TB
    subgraph Control["Control plane — cloud"]
        API[API and playback service]
        AUTH[Auth and entitlements]
        REC[Recommendations]
        STEER[Steering service<br/>which OCA should this client use]
    end
    subgraph Encode["Content pipeline"]
        SRC[Studio master] --> ENC[Encoder farm<br/>many bitrate ladders]
        ENC --> ORIGIN[(Origin storage)]
    end
    ORIGIN -. off-peak fill .-> OCA
    CLIENT[Player] --> API
    API --> STEER
    STEER --> CLIENT
    CLIENT -- segments over HTTP --> OCA[(Open Connect appliance<br/>inside the ISP)]

⚠️ Separate the control plane from the data plane and say so. Browsing, auth, recommendations and steering are ordinary microservices in the cloud. The video bytes never touch them. That split is the answer to "how do you serve this much traffic" — you don't, the edge does.

Adaptive bitrate, precisely

The file is encoded once into a ladder of renditions and cut into segments of a few seconds. A manifest lists them. The player measures throughput and buffer level and picks the next segment's rendition — so adaptation is client-side, per segment, requiring no server state.

Decision Choice Why
Streaming protocol HTTP segments (DASH/HLS) Plain HTTP caches in any CDN; a custom protocol does not
Adaptation Client-side per segment Server-side adaptation needs per-session state and cannot see the client's buffer
Encoding Per-title ladders, offline One-size ladders waste bitrate on simple content
Placement Predictive fill off-peak Demand-fill means the first viewers of a new release all miss

Failure modes

  • OCA fails or is saturated — steering must return an alternative, and the player must survive a mid-stream switch.
  • A new release everyone wants at 9pm — the fill window is the mitigation; if it did not run, you have a correlated miss across every ISP at once.
  • Encoder backlog — a title is licensed but not encoded. Catalogue must reflect availability, not intent.

4. Google Maps — routing

Requirements

Functional Non-functional
Fastest route between two points Planet-scale graph — hundreds of millions of nodes
Live traffic affecting the answer Sub-100 ms query
Turn-by-turn navigation, rerouting Answers must be correct, not approximate

The hard problem

Dijkstra on a continental road graph explores millions of nodes per query. At Maps' query volume that is impossible — so you must precompute.

Road networks are strongly hierarchical: a motorway junction matters far more than a cul-de-sac. Contraction Hierarchies exploits this. In a preprocessing pass, nodes are contracted in ascending order of importance — removed from the graph, with shortcut edges inserted between their neighbours to preserve exact shortest distances [7][8]. At query time a bidirectional search runs upward from both ends through the hierarchy and meets in the middle, touching a tiny fraction of the graph while still returning the exact shortest path [7][9].

flowchart LR
    subgraph Pre["Preprocessing — hours, offline"]
        G[Road graph] --> ORDER[Order nodes by importance]
        ORDER --> CONTRACT[Contract nodes<br/>insert shortcut edges]
        CONTRACT --> CH[(Contracted graph)]
    end
    subgraph Query["Query — milliseconds"]
        S[Origin] --> FWD[Forward search<br/>upward only]
        T[Destination] --> BWD[Backward search<br/>upward only]
        FWD --> MEET[Meet in the middle]
        BWD --> MEET
        MEET --> PATH[Unpack shortcuts<br/>into real roads]
    end
    CH --> FWD
    CH --> BWD

⚠️ The trap is live traffic. Contraction Hierarchies precomputes against fixed edge weights. Traffic changes them continuously, and re-running preprocessing takes hours. Real systems handle this with time-dependent or customisable variants that split preprocessing into a slow topology phase and a fast weight phase [8], so a weight update costs seconds rather than hours. Saying "CH assumes static weights, so live traffic needs a customisable variant" is the senior answer.

Decisions

Decision Choice Why not the alternative
Algorithm Precomputed hierarchy + bidirectional search Plain Dijkstra is far too slow; plain A* helps but not enough on continental graphs
Exactness Exact An approximate route that misses a motorway is obviously wrong to the user
Traffic Separate fast weight-customisation phase Full re-preprocessing takes hours
Sharding By geographic region, with boundary nodes A single global graph does not fit one machine

5. Live location tracking and dispatch (Uber-style)

Requirements

Functional Non-functional
Drivers publish location every few seconds Millions of concurrent location writes
Riders see nearby drivers live "Find nearest driver" in well under a second
Match a rider to a driver Matching must not double-assign one driver
Live ETA and trip tracking Location data is high-volume and short-lived

The hard problem

"Find me the nearest available driver" is a geospatial query at write-heavy scale. Computing distance to every driver is O(n) per request and hopeless. You need a spatial index — and the index is being rewritten constantly, because every driver moves every few seconds.

Uber's answer is H3, a hierarchical hexagonal grid that models the Earth as a subdivided icosahedron rather than a lat/long plane [10][11]. Each location maps to a cell id, so "nearby" becomes a lookup of a handful of cell ids rather than a scan. At resolution 8 a cell is roughly 0.74 km², and a search checks the cell plus its neighbours [12].

Why hexagons rather than squares: every hexagon's six neighbours are equidistant from its centre [10][11]. A square grid has neighbours at two different distances — edge-adjacent and corner-adjacent — so "within one ring" means two different real distances depending on direction. That distortion matters when you are choosing who is closest.

flowchart TB
    D[Driver app<br/>location every 4s] --> ING[Location ingest<br/>write-optimised]
    ING --> GEO[(Geo index<br/>H3 cell to driver ids<br/>in memory, TTL'd)]
    ING --> STREAM[[Location stream]]
    STREAM --> TRIP[(Trip store<br/>durable history)]
    R[Rider app] --> MATCH[Matching service]
    MATCH --> GEO
    MATCH --> OFFER[Offer to driver<br/>with a lock and timeout]
    OFFER --> D
    STREAM --> ETA[ETA service] --> R

Decisions

Decision Choice Why not the alternative
Spatial index Hexagonal cell id (H3) Geohash squares distort neighbour distance; quadtrees rebalance badly under constant writes
Index storage In-memory, TTL'd A durable database cannot take millions of overwrites per second, and stale locations are worthless anyway
Location history Separate append-only stream Mixing the hot index with durable history couples two very different workloads
Assignment Lock the driver, offer with a timeout Optimistic assignment double-books; a held lock without a timeout strands the driver
Sharding By cell id Sharding by driver id scatters a "nearby" query across every shard

⚠️ Matching is a distributed-locking problem wearing a geospatial hat. Two riders can be nearest to the same driver simultaneously. You need a single owner per driver — usually the shard that owns their cell — and an offer that expires, so a driver who does not respond is released rather than lost.

Failure modes

  • A driver's connection drops — their location goes stale. TTL the index entry so they age out rather than being offered a ride they cannot see.
  • Cell hotspot — a stadium at closing time puts a hundred thousand riders in one cell. Needs finer resolution in dense areas, which is exactly what a hierarchical index gives you.
  • Clock skew — location timestamps from client devices cannot be trusted for ordering.

6. A payment system — exactly-once with real money

Worth including because the constraint is unlike the others: correctness beats availability, and the failure mode is financial rather than a slow page.

The hard problem

A network call to a payment provider can time out after the charge succeeded. You cannot tell the difference between "declined" and "succeeded but the response was lost". Retrying naively double-charges.

Three mechanisms, together:

  1. Client-supplied idempotency key — the same key returns the same result rather than charging again.
  2. Transactional outbox — the state change and the intent-to-call commit in one database transaction, so you can never have one without the other (14 §4).
  3. Double-entry ledger — every movement is two balanced rows. The invariant "all entries sum to zero" is checkable, and a violated invariant is detectable rather than silent.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Payment API
    participant D as Database
    participant O as Outbox relay
    participant P as Provider
    C->>A: "charge request with Idempotency-Key: abc123"
    A->>D: "BEGIN, insert payment (unique on key), insert outbox row, COMMIT"
    A-->>C: 202 Accepted with payment id
    O->>D: poll outbox
    O->>P: "authorise, idempotency key = payment id"
    P-->>O: authorised or declined
    O->>D: "update state, write ledger entries, enqueue next event"
    C->>A: poll or webhook for final state

⚠️ Note the API returns 202 Accepted, not 200 with a final answer. Pretending a distributed, retryable operation is synchronous is how double-charges happen.

Decision Choice Why
Idempotency Unique constraint on the key, in the same transaction A cache check outside the transaction races
Provider call Async via outbox relay An in-request call that times out leaves indeterminate state
Money representation Integer minor units, or decimal double cannot represent 0.10 — never use it for money
Consistency Strong for the ledger Eventual consistency on balances means the number shown is a guess
Reconciliation Daily against provider statements Any distributed system drifts — detect it deliberately

7. The patterns underneath

Read across the six and the same handful of ideas keep appearing. That is what to demonstrate.

Pattern Where it shows up
Precompute the expensive thing Instagram feeds, Maps contraction, Netflix fill windows
Split control plane from data plane Netflix bytes vs browsing, Uber index vs trip history
Push work to the edge Netflix OCAs, CDN for Instagram media
Hybrid strategies beat pure ones Instagram push/pull; nothing real is purely one thing
At-least-once plus idempotency WhatsApp receipts, payments, every queue
Bound anything unbounded Capped feeds, TTL'd locations, expiring offers
Index for the query you actually run H3 cells for "nearby", capped feed for "my timeline"

And the estimation discipline from 08 §2 applies to all of them: state your assumptions, do the arithmetic out loud, and let the numbers pick the design.

8. Checklist before you answer any of these

  • Restated requirements and asked which non-functional one dominates
  • Did the arithmetic — QPS, storage, bandwidth — before drawing anything
  • Named the one hard problem rather than drawing boxes uniformly
  • Gave a decision with its alternative and why it loses
  • Said the failure modes unprompted
  • Mentioned what you would monitor
  • Was explicit about what you are not solving in scope

Sources

  5. Instagram Supercharges Cassandra with a Pluggable RocksDB Storage Engine — The New Stack
  6. How Instagram is scaling its infrastructure across the ocean — Opensource.com
  7. Contraction hierarchies — Wikipedia

  10. H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index — Uber Engineering
